title: Why Did Joseph Choose Forgiveness Over Revenge?
paragraphs:
Why Did Joseph Choose Forgiveness Over Revenge?
The Man Who Had Every Reason to Destroy His Enemies—Yet Chose Grace Instead
There are moments in life when pain does not merely wound us—it rewrites us.
A betrayal. A lie. A family member who turned against you. A friend who abandoned you. A person who smiled to your face while secretly digging your grave.
But Joseph understood something even harder.
He understood what it feels like to suffer because of the people you loved most.
And that is why his story still reaches into human hearts thousands of years later.
Because Joseph is not merely a Bible character.
Joseph is every person who has ever asked:
"Why did they do this to me?"
"What do I do with all this pain?"
Joseph was the favored son of Jacob. Scripture tells us his father loved him deeply and gave him a special tunic.
His brothers hated him for it.
What began as jealousy eventually became something darker.
Genesis 37 records one of the most chilling family betrayals in Scripture.
His brothers stripped him of his robe.
Then sold him into slavery for twenty pieces of silver.
The Hebrew text uses the word בּוֹר (bor) for "pit."
A place where nobody hears your cries.
Watching dust rise behind the caravan carrying him into slavery.
Many people believe their greatest pain came from strangers.
Yet one of the most remarkable truths in the Joseph narrative appears repeatedly.
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say God prevented the pit.
It does not say God prevented slavery.
It does not say God prevented prison.
It says God was with him.
Many people assume God's presence means protection from suffering.
God's presence often means companionship through suffering.
Years later, Joseph would rise from prisoner to ruler.
From slave to second-in-command over Egypt.
The very brothers who sold him now stood before him.
Unaware they were standing before the brother they betrayed.
This is the moment every wounded heart understands.
The moment when revenge becomes possible.
The moment when the balance shifts.
The moment you can finally make them feel what they made you feel.
Joseph possessed the authority to imprison them.
Nobody would have called it unjust.
Yet Joseph chose something that still shocks humanity.
The answer lies in one of the most profound statements in all of Scripture.
"וְאַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה"
Ve'atem chashavtem alai ra'ah, Elohim chashavah letovah.
"You intended evil against me, but God intended it for good."
Notice Joseph does not deny evil.
He does not call evil good.
He acknowledges evil for what it was.
Yet he saw another hand moving behind human evil.
Joseph realized something most people never discover.
If God is truly sovereign, then your story belongs ultimately to God—not your enemies.
Your betrayers may write a chapter.
But they cannot write the ending.
This truth becomes even more powerful when viewed through the lens of Jesus Christ.
Joseph was betrayed by his brothers.
Jesus was betrayed by His own disciple.
Joseph descended into suffering before exaltation.
Jesus descended into suffering before resurrection glory.
Joseph saved nations through his suffering.
Jesus saved humanity through His suffering.
The Greek New Testament records Jesus praying from the cross:
Joseph's story points forward to Christ.
The Savior who took humanity's betrayal and transformed it into salvation.
This is why forgiveness is not weakness.
Biblical forgiveness is one of the strongest acts a human being can perform.
Forgiveness does not mean trust must instantly return.
Forgiveness means surrendering judgment into God's hands.
"Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God."
Many people spend years rehearsing offenses.
Waiting for apologies that never come.
The bitterness becomes its own prison.
The brothers who sold him were no longer controlling his life.
Why continue allowing them to control his heart?
Perhaps that is exactly where many readers find themselves today.
Maybe somebody caused wounds that still ache years later.
Joseph's story does not ask you to pretend the pain never happened.
It invites you to see something bigger.
The God who worked in Joseph's pit is still working today.
The God who worked through slavery is still working today.
The God who worked through prison is still working today.
The God who transformed betrayal into blessing is still working today.
The chapter you are living in is not the final chapter.
And when God writes endings, redemption is never off the table.
This is the heartbeat of our message:
And above all, because that is the Gospel.
The scandal of sin became the miracle of salvation.
If this article stirred your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
Because someone else's healing may begin with a message you chose to share.
Because someone's salvation story may start with a post you refused to keep to yourself.
Because the pit was never Joseph's destination.
And your current chapter is not yours either.
The enemy may have written the scandal.
But Jesus still writes the ending.
